claims.text: Moderate lattice strain produces a high density of undercoordinated Pt sites in platinum-group-metal nanoscale catalysts.
Lattice strain modulates the adsorption energies of catalytic intermediates.
The strain-induced adsorption/desorption balance minimizes poisoning by strongly bound ethanol-oxidation intermediates.
Strain-induced intermediate management lowers ethanol-oxidation onset potential and increases current density.
Strain-induced intermediate management improves catalyst durability during ethanol oxidation.
Controlled thermal annealing induces moderate surface lattice strain relative to an unannealed catalyst.
Surface lattice strain shifts the Pt d-band center.
Surface lattice strain increases the number of undercoordinated Pt active sites.
Undercoordinated Pt sites can enhance catalytic activity through their distinct adsorption geometry.
Strain-induced electronic modifications weaken the binding of CO and partially oxidized poisoning intermediates.
Weaker poisoning-intermediate binding facilitates the sequential complete oxidation of ethanol to CO2.
The strained catalyst will have a lower onset potential and higher current density than the unannealed catalyst under identical ethanol-oxidation conditions.
The strained catalyst will exhibit greater selectivity toward complete ethanol-oxidation products.
The strained catalyst will have greater operational durability than the unannealed catalyst.
The proposed strain effect applies under moderate strain in alkaline media.
Excessive strain may reverse the beneficial effect by causing intermediate over-binding or structural destabilization.
The mechanism may not apply in neutral or acidic media.
The quantitative relationships among strain, d-band shift, and ethanol-intermediate binding energies remain undetermined.

contradictions.description: The boundary explicitly predicts that excessive strain may degrade performance, while the falsification rule treats performance degradation with increased strain as falsifying the mechanism without restricting that criterion to the moderate-strain regime.
